{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=algorithmic+mechanisms+accountability+autonomous+systems+consequence+tracking+decision+trees&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.62311/nesx/rb-69ag-978-81-68314-31-3\", \"title\": [\"Computational Law and Responsible AI Governance for Algorithmic Accountability, Digital Rights and Autonomous Decision Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Abstract\\nComputational law can help translate selected norms and institutional duties into reviewable decision processes, while autonomous AI systems raise new questions about authority, evidence and remedy. This monograph develops a research framework for algorithmic accountability, digital rights and responsible governance using only relevant works in the supplied reference corpus. Ten themes cover machine-readable norms, effective remedies, lifecycle responsibility, causal impact assessment, explanation, model drift, generative provenance, policy-as-code, auditability and sectoral assurance. Five chapters progress from legal and institutional foundations to distributional evaluation, model and agent assurance, reproducible operations and applied governance. The central object is a consequential decision whose governing rule, evidence, model state, human intervention and avenue of challenge can be reconstructed. Proposed outputs include norm-to-code matrices, impact taxonomies, dated rollout panels, reason-giving tests, bounded agent manifests, policy registers and disputed-case audit packets. The framework distinguishes technical validation from legal authorization and preserves local interpretation across jurisdictions. It assesses whether a person can receive notice, correct evidence, contest an outcome and obtain a meaningful remedy under ordinary operating conditions. Public services, financial scoring and autonomous mobility provide contrasting research settings; no proposed experiment is described as an observed result. Independent review, counterexamples, incident recovery and longitudinal appeal evidence anchor the account of trustworthy deployment. The resulting evidence standard links computational methods to institutional duties without treating code as self-authorizing law.\\nKeywords\\ncomputational law, responsible AI, algorit…

{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=algorithmic+accountability+and+consequence+tracking+in+multi-agent+decision+systems&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Artificial Intelligence and the Ethical Foundations of Cardiothoracic Surgery: Evidence, Accountability, and the Limits of Delegated Judgment.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving rapidly from retrospective prediction and image analysis into treatment selection, operative planning, intraoperative guidance, and postoperative prognostication in cardiothoracic surgery. This transition raises an ethical problem that cannot be resolved by model accuracy alone: when an algorithm begins to shape a high-stakes clinical decision, the distribution of knowledge, authority, and responsibility also changes. This review synthesizes cardiothoracic and closely related medical evidence available through August 2026, with emphasis on quantitative performance, human-AI interaction, bias, patient autonomy, and liability. The available evidence is simultaneously encouraging and cautionary. Machine-learning approaches can improve predictive performance and AI-assisted thoracic planning can reduce errors and increase procedural consistency; however, these gains have not consistently translated into superior patient outcomes. Human-AI studies similarly demonstrate that improved accuracy may coexist with automation bias and overacceptance of algorithmic recommendations. Evidence of demographic performance disparities and limitations in the representativeness of training and validation datasets further raises concerns regarding fairness and equitable access to care. On this basis, we argue that cardiothoracic AI should be governed according to the level of decision influence rather than by technology type alone. We distinguish non-delegable professional duties, distributed system responsibilities, and non-transferable patient authority, and propose an Ethical Heart Team Framework for converting algorithmic output into ethically defensible clinical action.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/medsci14050586\", \"pmid\": \"42783459\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13609802\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availab…

id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2302.07344v1
published: 2023-02-14T21:08:52Z
summary: In-situ visual observations of marine organisms is crucial to developing behavioural understandings and their relations to their surrounding ecosystem. Typically, these observations are collected via divers, tags, and remotely-operated or human-piloted vehicles. Recently, however, autonomous underwater vehicles equipped with cameras and embedded computers with GPU capabilities are being developed for a variety of applications, and in particular, can be used to supplement these existing data collection mechanisms where human operation or tags are more difficult. Existing approaches have focused on using fully-supervised tracking methods, but labelled data for many underwater species are severely lacking. Semi-supervised trackers may offer alternative tracking solutions because they require less data than fully-supervised counterparts. However, because there are not existing realistic underwater tracking datasets, the performance of semi-supervised tracking algorithms in the marine domain is not well understood. To better evaluate their performance and utility, in this paper we provide (1) a novel dataset specific to marine animals located at http://warp.whoi.edu/vmat/, (2) an evaluation of state-of-the-art semi-supervised algorithms in the context of underwater animal tracking, and (3) an evaluation of real-world performance through demonstrations using a semi-supervised algorithm on-board an autonomous underwater vehicle to track marine animals in the wild.
